summary:
Florida stands under the United States national framework, which sets the sharpest documentary risk for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker; new passports are issued only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, and passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and in November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the department's restrictions to take effect, superseding a policy in place since 1992.

Entry adds a second exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement banning trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sporting events, with visa applicants flagged by an internal marking; applicants who list a gender other than sex assigned at birth are treated as grounds for a permanent ban for fraud. Several foreign governments responded, with advisories issued in April 2025 about trans people travelling to the United States and at least eight European states adjusting their guidance for trans and nonbinary citizens in March 2025.

Florida's own restrictions operate through Fla. Stat. 553.865, the 2023 restroom and changing-facility law. It applies only to buildings owned or leased by state or local government: state offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons and jails, local immigration detention, state parks and toll-road plazas. The statute purports to cover all schools, public and private. Refusing to leave a sex-segregated restroom or changing facility within its scope can be charged as criminal trespass. Private businesses fall outside its scope, and the ACLU advises fact-specific judgment and legal counsel in borderline settings.

The law produced its first known arrest on 19 March 2025, when Marcy Rheintgen, a 20-year-old transgender college student, washed her hands in a women's restroom at the Florida State Capitol after police were alerted in advance. She had announced publicly that she was there to break the law. The misdemeanor trespass charge carried up to 60 days in jail. On 20 June 2025 Leon County Judge Lashawn Riggans dismissed the case, holding that as a defendant charged under the statute she had no standing to argue that the law itself was illegitimate, so its substance was never tested in court. At least 14 states have adopted comparable laws barring trans women from women's bathrooms at schools and some government buildings.

Florida scores 8.0 on the national anti-trans law scale and is labelled Do Not Travel for trans people, with 3.7 trans women murdered per 100,000 per year. A national analysis of 2008–2025 data found that state law severity does not correlate with killing rates across the 26 states with data, the trendline nearly flat. Legal climate and street-level violence are separate visitor risks, and a permissive legal environment should not be read as a signal of personal safety.

Visitors who are detained face documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In immigration custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse.

Equality Florida took the unprecedented step on 12 April 2023 of issuing a travel advisory warning of risks to the health, safety and freedom of people considering short or long-term travel or relocation to Florida, citing hostile LGBTQ laws alongside reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks and book bans. The organisation reports cancellations of events and conferences and notes the US military considering redeployment for service members' families.
tangentialFactors:
Florida's bathroom statute sits inside a wider national pattern: a Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states, while 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances.

Document rules are tightening elsewhere in the country. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing trans people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences, invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups describe it as a template for other states, with further bills pending. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest Do Not Travel state for trans people, bringing the total to four.

Care access nationally is constrained. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as mutilation, leading some hospitals to pause care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court, and litigation is ongoing.

Hostility at federal level has escalated into enforcement rhetoric. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting radical gender ideology and characterised as domestic terrorist groups; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy prioritised identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology was described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist. Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.
localsOnly:
The 2023 facility statute binds Florida residents and visitors identically, and its reach is defined by building ownership rather than by who is using the restroom. Residents employed in state offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons and jails, local immigration detention, state parks and toll-road plazas encounter it daily; the same law is asserted to cover students in every public and private school in the state.

Because the 2025 dismissal turned on standing rather than on the merits, the statute has never been substantively upheld or struck down, and residents challenging an arrest have no established route to attack the law itself through that charge.

Equality Florida's advisory addresses relocation as well as travel, and its warning about risks to health, safety and freedom applies to people moving to the state on a permanent basis.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved and not sourced here: whether Florida has enacted its own restrictions on changing sex markers on birth certificates or driver's licences, and whether state law bars gender-affirming care for minors. The inventory supplies national figures for both questions but no Florida-specific statute or rule.

Unresolved: the enforcement frequency of the 2023 facility statute outside the 2025 Capitol incident. The single documented arrest involved a protester who announced the action in advance and was arrested with police alerted beforehand; no sourced data shows how often the law is applied to ordinary restroom use.

Unresolved: whether Florida provides hate-crime enhancement or any statutory protection for trans people targeted on the basis of gender identity, and how state prosecutors treat anti-trans assaults. The murder figure of 3.7 per 100,000 per year is reported without a sourced methodology, time window or comparison to national rates.

Unresolved: the final outcome of the ACLU's challenge to the federal passport policy and of the various federal measures that have been blocked or enjoined, several of which remain in litigation.
